items.content: He sits at the counter long after the other booths have emptied, turning his coffee cup slowly in both hands as though it might tell him something. The waitress wipes the same stretch of laminate over and over, not unkindly, while the cook rattles pans in the back with the deliberate noise of a man ready to go home. Outside, the parking lot holds nothing but orange light and an old receipt skidding across asphalt. He knows he should leave, but leaving means deciding where.

items.content: The train lurches forward with a groan, pressing bodies together like pages in a swollen book. Somewhere behind her, a man exhales coffee breath into the stale air, while overhead fluorescent lights flicker their indifferent morse code. She grips the cold pole and watches faces — blank, inward, quietly enduring — each one a sealed envelope she will never open. The city moves beneath them all, indifferent and relentless, carrying its passengers nowhere they truly want to go.

items.content: The coffee had been brewing since before anyone thought to wake, its dark breath spreading through the empty kitchen like a slow rumor. Morning light came in sideways, pale and uncertain, laying itself across the linoleum in long yellow strips. There was something almost tender about the stillness — the gurgling machine, the rising steam, the smell that promised warmth before warmth had arrived. It was the house speaking to itself, the way houses do before the day claims them.
